BB.name: BetterBench
BB.citation: Reuel et al., BetterBench, NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks; arXiv 2411.12990
BB.source: Appendix I.1 template and the public database page (betterbench.stanford.edu/database.html), criterion names as shown per benchmark
BB.answer_scale: 0 not acknowledged and not addressed; 5 acknowledged but not addressed; 10 partially addressed; 15 fully addressed; n/a not relevant (Appendix F)
BB.missing_information_rule: A criterion that is neither acknowledged nor addressed receives 0; mentioned but not provided receives 5; not relevant receives n/a and is excluded from averages (Appendix F).
BB.reuse_terms: Assessments released under CC BY 4.0 (Appendix I.2). Paper text under arXiv terms; criterion names are short phrases.

ECBD.name: ECBD worksheet
ECBD.citation: Liu et al., ECBD: Evidence-Centered Benchmark Design for NLP, ACL 2024; arXiv 2406.08723
ECBD.answer_scale: Free text per question; questions come in describe, justify, support triples per module
ECBD.missing_information_rule: No scoring. A describe question records what the creators state; a justify question records their reasons; a support question records the validity evidence offered. Absence of evidence is recorded as absence, not as a score.
ECBD.reuse_terms: No license file in the repository. Repository file may be used with the authors' permission (given to the author, 31 October 2026); verbatim text may appear in prompts and in the public package with attribution. Nothing beyond the repository files was shared.

SC.name: Scorecard of AI Benchmark Quality
SC.citation: San Joaquin, Gipiskis and Chin, EvalEval 2026, pages 128 to 160; DOI 10.18653/v1/2026.evaleval-1.25
SC.source: Appendix A.2 Quality Dimensions (final version); local text literature/slr-2026-10-28/texts/R097.txt
SC.answer_scale: Each item satisfied, unsatisfied or not applicable, with a justification; each dimension scored 1 to 4 from the severity of unsatisfied items; classes A to E from dimension scores (Appendix A.1, Section 5)
SC.missing_information_rule: Vague or absent documentation can make an item unsatisfied; a baseline item unsatisfied makes the dimension unscorable and the evaluation invalid (Appendix A.1). Not applicable is allowed with a reason.
SC.reuse_terms: ACL Anthology publication; check the PDF footer for the license before copying item text.

H2B.name: How2Bench
H2B.citation: Cao et al., How Should I Build A Benchmark? Revisiting Code-Related Benchmarks For LLMs; later titled Position: Code Benchmarks Should Prioritize Rigor, Reliability, and Reproducibility; arXiv 2501.10711
H2B.source: Printable checklist Figures/How2Bench-full-new.pdf and Figures/new_checklist/1-5.png in the arXiv source; 55 numbered criteria with priority stars
H2B.answer_scale: Checkbox per criterion; priority three stars highly important, two stars important, one star optional. In the authors' profiling study each criterion was labelled present or not mentioned (Section 7.3).
H2B.missing_information_rule: A benchmark is labelled as not considering a step unless the paper contains explicit textual evidence of it; not mentioned is grouped with not done (Sections 4.2 and 7.3).
H2B.reuse_terms: arXiv paper; the checklist is a figure. Check the arXiv license statement on the abstract page before copying.

ABC.name: Agentic Benchmark Checklist
ABC.citation: Zhu et al., Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks, NeurIPS 2025; arXiv 2507.02825
ABC.source: ABC.md in github.com/uiuc-kang-lab/agentic-benchmarks (item wording) and Section 4 of the paper (identifiers T, O, R)
ABC.missing_information_rule: An item the benchmark does not document or address receives 0 with a short reason (Appendix D reports). No separate category for missing information.
ABC.reuse_terms: No license file in the repository; arXiv paper. Repository file may be used with the authors' permission (given to the author, 31 October 2026); verbatim text may appear in prompts and in the public package with attribution. Nothing beyond the repository files was shared. The two paraphrased items (T.6, O.f.1) come from the paper, not the repository file.

CAL.name: Benchmark Caliper
CAL.citation: Corona, Truong, Trager and others; repository github.com/aims-foundations/benchmark-caliper; paper listed as Uplifting Human Decision Making in AI Evaluation by Automating Benchmark Validity Analysis (ICML 2026 workshop) and in the framework file as Validity Analysis when Porting Benchmarks Across Cultures and Regions
CAL.source: framework.yaml in the repository: six dimensions, each with definition, checklist items and a 1 to 5 scoring rubric
CAL.answer_scale: 1 to 5 per dimension: 1 major validity violations; 2 significant concerns; 3 partially addressed; 4 well addressed; 5 fully addressed. Item scoring returns Unknown when evidence is insufficient.
CAL.missing_information_rule: Unknown is returned when evidence is insufficient for an item; at dimension level the rubric scores documented awareness, so silence lowers the score.
CAL.reuse_terms: No license file in the repository. Repository file may be used with the authors' permission (given to the author, 31 October 2026); verbatim text may appear in prompts and in the public package with attribution. Nothing beyond the repository files was shared.
CAL.note: Every item presumes a stated target deployment context. Mapped for coverage only after HELM was removed on 31 October 2026.

OECD.name: OECD facets
OECD.citation: Cohn and Hernandez-Orallo, A framework for characterising evaluation instruments of AI performance, chapter 6 of AI and the Future of Skills, Volume 2, OECD 2023, DOI 10.1787/a9fe53cb-en; earlier Cohn et al., A Framework for Categorising AI Evaluation Instruments, IJCAI-ECAI 2022 workshop, CEUR-WS Vol-3169 paper 3, CC BY 4.0
OECD.source: Chapter 6, section Characterising AI evaluation instruments; local text literature/slr-2026-10-28/texts/S05.txt lines 4520 to 4590
OECD.answer_scale: One categorical value per facet from the listed values; some values require a free text specification
OECD.missing_information_rule: Reliability allows N/A when the testing methodology or common use is not clear. Other facets have no missing value; raters choose from the listed values.
OECD.reuse_terms: OECD publication terms for the chapter; the 2022 workshop paper is CC BY 4.0.
OECD.note: A classification. Only facets with a preferred value enter agreement and missing information results; the others are reported as a description and feed the new rubric's description part.

items.text: Who/What are the intended objects of evaluation?
What is the intended use of the benchmark? Who are the intended users of the benchmark?
DESCRIBE: i) What are the capabilities of interest? ii) How is each one defined, and under what context is each one defined?
JUSTIFY: How are the capabilities of interest connected to the intended use of the benchmark (specified in Q2)? Are the capabilities theoretically attainable by the objects to be evaluated?
SUPPORT: What validity evidence do the benchmark creators offer to support the choice and definition of capabilities of interest?
DESCRIBE: i) Characterize the test items. ii) Which capabilities of interest does each test item aim to capture?
JUSTIFY: How does each test item elicit evidence about its target capabilities? Justify via the characteristics of the test items (Q6).
SUPPORT: What evidence do the benchmark creators offer to support content validity of the test items?
DESCRIBE: Given an input, how are the objects of evaluation adapted or instructed to provide the output?
JUSTIFY: Elaborate on the suitability of the adaptation methods for all intended objects of evaluation.
SUPPORT: What validity evidence do benchmark designers offer that supports the choice of the adaptation methods?
DESCRIBE: How many test items are chosen to assemble the subset used for evaluation? What factors inform this selection?
JUSTIFY: How does the described assembly method ensure that the produced subset elicits sufficient evidence for all capabilities of interest?
SUPPORT: What validity evidence do the benchmark creators offer to support the choice of assembly methods?
DESCRIBE: For each test item, i) What responses are captured and used for evidence extraction? ii) How is evidence extracted and represented?
JUSTIFY: How does the extracted evidence capture the capabilities of interest?
SUPPORT: What validity evidence do the benchmark creators offer to support the choice of evidence extraction method?
DESCRIBE: How is the evidence accumulated to draw insights about the objects of evaluation in terms of capabilities of interest?
JUSTIFY: How does the method of accumulating evidence capture capabilities of interest?
SUPPORT: What validity evidence do the benchmark creators offer to support the choice of evidence accumulation method?

items.text: Flaw mitigation
Describe steps to prevent, identify, and correct for flaws in evaluation

For each unavoidable flaw: (a) explain qualitatively what it is and which direction it likely biases results, (b) quantify its impact where possible (e.g. ground truth noise), and (c) provide explicit guidance on which conclusions from the evaluation remain valid despite the flaw and which do not
Interpretation of methodology and results
Report relevant baselines, especially human baselines for human-centric tasks
Report performance of minimal baselines (e.g. random selection, majority-class prediction, zero-shot naive models) to establish a lower bound and give context for model scores
Annotated ground truth is verified robustly, whether annotated by humans or AI

If using model rater(s), document evidence that ratings correlate with human judgments; design the rater to resist adversarial inputs and reward hacking; verify consistency of model rater across repeated identical inputs; identify and mitigate systematic biases in the model rater
Multiple annotators label each item independently, with inter-annotator agreement reported (e.g. Cohen's kappa >= 0.7), or a programmatic verification method with documented accuracy is used
Each task has a verified end state, whether it is solvable or not
Classify each task as solvable or intentionally unsolvable, and document the expected model behavior for each type
For solvable tasks, provide verified ground-truth solutions
Enumerate all valid solution forms, or specify acceptance criteria broad enough to recognize equivalent correct answers

The scoring implementation must not be exploitable through shortcuts such as outputting trigger strings, exploiting parser edge cases, or matching answer patterns without completing the underlying task
Scoring rules are well-specified and handle edge-case outputs such as partial answers, correct answers in unexpected formats, and refusals
Validate that the automated output parser produces consistent results on identical inputs
Measure parser accuracy against a set of manually verified outputs
Conduct adversarial testing of the scoring pipeline to verify it cannot be gamed without the model completing the task

Consider whether sufficient LLMs are evaluated.
Consider whether representative LLMs (e.g., covering latest/classical LLM families, small/large LLMs, and open-/closed-source LLMs) are evaluated.
Consider whether the prompt is of high quality (e.g., the instruction and intent are clear).
The prompts have been validated by humans or LLMs (e.g., evaluated or discussed by participants or preliminarily tried out on several LLMs).
Try different paraphrases of the prompt.
Try different prompting strategies to observe the impact on the evaluation results (e.g., in-context learning, chain-of-thought).
Pay attention to the hardware environment (such as GPU card, storage size, etc.) of the experiment.
Pay attention to the operating system and software environment (e.g. operating system, version, etc.) used for the experiment.
Pay attention to the off-the-shelf platforms, frameworks, or libraries for LLM evaluation (e.g., fast chat, vllm, huggingface) that are used.
Repeat the experiment multiple times to reduce the impact of randomness on the evaluation.
Consider various randomization strategies (e.g., trying various temperature parameters) to reduce the impact of parameter configuration on the evaluation.
Record the experimental process in detail (e.g., parameter settings, running time, input/output pairs, etc.).
Observe the difficulty of the benchmark, checking if the benchmark is too hard or too easy for LLMs (i.e., most LLMs score too high/low).
Consider whether the benchmark can distinguish the pros and cons of different LLMs.
If the experiment is repeated several times, consider the stability of the benchmark (i.e., whether the experimental results vary too much in the repeated experiments).

Analyze the correlation between the data and their score. For example, if there is a correlation between the data (such as similar difficulty and knowledge required), then the scores should also be correlated.

items.text: does the evaluation instrument just measure observed (aggregated) performance on a TASK (e.g. protein folding, credit scoring) or can the evaluation instrument also measure a CAPABILITY (e.g. object permanence, dealing with negation)?

items.text: does the evaluation instrument cover a BIASED or unbiased (REPRESENTATIVE) distribution of what is meant to be measured?
items.answerable_from_inputs: partly: the 2023 raters needed literature beyond the specification for Coverage and Specificity

items.text: is the benchmark meant to foster research or development, or to certify whether an AI system conforms with some level or standard?

to what extent is the evaluation instrument a toy problem or a complex gamified problem? Is it a realistic setting (e.g. a simulated scenario, a lab or testing facility) or is the evaluation itself happening in real life?
are results reported as an absolute metric (criterion-referenced) or are they reported as a relative (percentage) metric to a reference (norm referenced), e.g. human performance?
are the results precisely aligned with what is meant to be measured or contaminated by other skills or tasks?
items.answerable_from_inputs: partly: the 2023 raters needed literature beyond the specification for Coverage and Specificity

items.text: is the analysis of results on the set of instances unstructured?; has the evaluation instrument identified a set of meta-features such as difficulty or dimension that could be used to analyse the results by these dimensions (ablatable)?; or are these meta-features used to adaptively or adversarially choose the instances to test more informatively (adaptive)?
items.answerable_from_inputs: partly: the 2023 raters needed literature beyond the specification for Coverage and Specificity

items.text: Once started, is the testing isolated from external factors or interference possibly affecting results (human participants, online data, weather, etc.)?; is there some partial interference not affecting the results significantly?; or is it dependent on external resources and conditions?
is scoring manual (e.g. through human questionnaires or judges) or automated (e.g. correct answers or optimality function) or a mixture?

does the evaluation present sufficient repetitions, episode length or number of instances to give low variance for the same subject when applied again (test-retest reliability)? If the testing methodology or the common use of the evaluation instrument is not clear, then N/A may be the most appropriate facet value.

is the evaluation non-reproducible, with results biased or spoiled if repeated?; does the evaluation instrument have stochastic components leading to different interactions?; or are the results completely reproducible, i.e. can the same exact test (inputs, interaction, etc.) be generated again for another (or the same) competitor?

is the evaluation based on fixed datasets?; have the instances been altered by adding post-processing variations (noise, rotations, etc.)?; or have the instances been created (e.g. using procedural generation)?
when the evaluation instrument was created, was it aiming at the short term (improving on the state of the art) or long term (more ambitious goals)?
items.answerable_from_inputs: partly: the 2023 raters needed literature beyond the specification for Coverage and Specificity

items.text: is it devised purposely for AI or adapted from tests designed to test humans?
is it measuring an autonomous system, coupled with other systems (e.g. humans) or as an isolated component?
is it loosely defined, customised to each participant or does the evaluation instrument have a predetermined independent specification?
does the evaluation instrument favour particular technologies, conditions or cultures that should not have an influence on the result of the evaluation?
Is the score measuring a capability at one moment or is it evaluating the development of the capability of the system within the test?
